catalog_quote: At a word level, nasalisation, tone patterns, and vowel harmony are phenomena which are treated as suprasegmentals. ... In this section, two suprasegmental aspects of language are treated: tone and intonation, and vowel harmony. 4.1 Tone and intonation Chakali is a tone language with both lexical and grammatical tone. Tones are distinctive pitch variations and are contrastive in the language since they can affect the meaning of words/phrases, where the words/phrases consist of exactly the same segmental sequences. ... An example of three different tonal melodies, using the minimal triplet, is ŋmɛ́ná 'okro', ŋmɛ́nà 'to cut' and ŋmɛ̀ná 'chisel'. ... Based on the evidence of nominal paradigms, two tones are suggested, i.e. high (H) and low (L). ... Since tones are assigned to moras, light syllables can get a single tone, i.e. H or L. audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal' (tonal-OR-pitch accent scope exit, no word stress) rests on the only published reference description of Chakali, Brindle 2017 (LangSci, open access), which we hold as publisher PDF + text; the deciding quotation is verbatim at sec. 4.1, pp. 294-295, and a full-text search confirms the phonology outline describes a two-tone (H/L) lexical+grammatical tone system with mora as TBU and never mentions stress or accent as a phonological category. Glottolog's descriptive bibliography and web searches turn up no competing or more specialised prosodic study (no phonology article, JIPA illustration, or instrumental work); the only unheld descriptive item is the author's own unpublished 2011 thesis, which the 2017 book is based on and supersedes. the first reader and the second reader (2026-09-12) already agreed; this reading re-confirmed the quote in the copy we hold.
